newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French tax hikes add limited cost to firms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French tax hikes add limited cost to firms.

text.p: The French government's imposition of higher taxes on companies will dent profits slightly in the short term but is not seen having a lasting negative impact on corporate performance, analysts and industry said on Monday.

"Our feeling here is that there will be a limited immediate impact on company profits. But at the same time it shows the government is comitted to EMU which is good for the (share) market," said JP Morgan market strategist Gary Dugan.
"The government aims to raise 22 billion francs ($3.6 billion) with the tax increase, that's some two to three percent of the total profits of CAC-40 companies," he added.

The French employers' federation CNPF, while expressing its disappointment about higher rates, said in a statement that the increases were only justified if they helped France to meet the target of European monetary union.

"The only counterparty is the creation of the euro, on January 1 1999, which is effectively an essential objective, on condition that French companies do not arrive exhausted," CNPF said in a statement. "The new taxes make no sense unless their exceptional character and their limited duration are cleary confirmed," it added.
Hugues de Montvallon, analyst at brokers Oddo, said he expected French shares to be four to five percent lower as a result of the tax increase.
The CAC 40 index of leading French shares stood at 2,869.73 points, down just 6.96 points or 0.2 percent at around 1430 gmt, having been as low as 2,830.68 during morning trading.
Former finance minister Jean Arthuis blasted the tax move.

"If one wants to fight unemployment, fight for job creation, you have to facilitate companies. They create wealth, they create jobs," he said. "The right policy, the only policy, is to cut public spending. It is not raising taxes," he said.

Nicolas Sarkozy, former budget minister and currently spokes-person for the RPR centre-right party, said "I do not believe in raising taxes to increase revenues. I remain convinced that, taking account of the rate of taxation in France, the way to raise tax revenues is to cut the tax rate."

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn announced two measures aimed at getting more revenues from the corporate sector to improve state finances in the run up to European economic and monetary union.
The main measure was a additional 15 percent surcharge on the corporate tax rate for the years 1997 and 1998 after which this special increase will come down to 10 percent.
The basic corporate tax rate is currently 33.3 percent of taxable profits. Since 1995 there has been a surcharge of 10 percent bringing the effective tax rate to 36.6 percent.

The extra surcharge of 15 percent of the basic tax rate, which will remain unchanged at 33.3 percent, will increase the surcharge to 25 percent and the effective tax rate for 1997 and 1998 to 41.6 percent. In 1999 and thereafter the effective rate will come down to 39.9 percent.
The tax rises will apply to companies with more than 50 million francs in annual turnover.

The other change announced by Strauss-Kahn concerns capital gains. These will no longer be taxed at 19 percent but the gains will be added to the total taxable profit and then taxed at the 41.6 percent rate.
French companies were reluctant to comment on the proposals.

"The tax increase will not hit us much. We are a multinational company and our sales and profits in France are only a small proportion of the total," said an official and a large insurance company who declined to be indentified.

Analysts said companies with a big exposure to France would be most hit. These are retailers, banks, some food companies and building companies. Traders said they expected companies such as hotels group Accor and bank BNP to be among the most heavy hit. BNP had no comment on the tax rises.
